title: Bialystoker Landsleit and the Postwar Community
summary: The landsleit organizations carried Bialystok’s communal bonds across continents and helped survivors rebuild connections and commemorate the destroyed city.

editorialContent:
![Białystok, the city remembered by its dispersed Jewish community](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Bazylika_w_Bia%C5%82ymstoku_-_Emilia_Ernst.jpg/1920px-Bazylika_w_Bia%C5%82ymstoku_-_Emilia_Ernst.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)
## A community rebuilt across distance

After the destruction of Jewish Białystok, community life did not simply end; it became dispersed. Survivors and earlier emigrants were separated across continents, but mutual aid, correspondence, publications and gatherings helped sustain a sense of belonging to one another and to their former home. The memorial book, *Byalisṭoḳer yizker bukh*, remembers that work through its accounts of the [Bialystoker Center in New York](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_40c66096cd327657b4c5c1d7), the [Bialystoker Relief Committee](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_515897af18a2c7413816bacd), and the [Bialystoker landsleit](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_3c320e9b086c613911be1ce4)—the people who shared a connection to Białystok.

The book’s story is one of continuity, but it is also a story of change. The prewar community in [Białystok](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_1fd067a7479a54f5797bfb15) had been destroyed, and survivors faced different needs in different places: emergency assistance, resettlement, work, communal institutions and remembrance. In New York, a pre-existing network of landsleit organizations could mobilize help. In other cities, smaller groups kept local connections alive. In Israel, survivors organized to help newcomers establish themselves and sought to build a settlement that would bear their hometown’s name.

The wider historical record establishes the scale of the catastrophe behind this effort. Before the war, Białystok was a major Jewish center; under German occupation, its Jews were confined in a ghetto, subjected to deportations and mass murder, and the ghetto was liquidated in 1943. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum’s account also describes survivors’ varied paths through the war and the city’s liberation in 1944. That history explains why postwar community-building had to begin among people scattered far beyond the city itself. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/bialystok?utm_source=openai))

## From relief work to a center

The memorial book traces the New York network back before the Holocaust. It says the Bialystoker Relief Committee was founded in America by David Sohn in 1919, with an early headquarters at 246 East Broadway. According to the book, the committee’s relief activity developed a social and communal life that eventually gave rise to the Bialystoker Center. Its institutional story is thus not simply a postwar response: the infrastructure that could serve survivors had grown out of decades of immigrant mutual aid.

In the book’s account, the Bialystoker Center reorganized relief work in 1945 for survivors still in Europe and helped Białystokers who arrived in the United States adjust to a new life. It also supported people settling elsewhere, including in Israel. A related passage describes survivors organizing in various American and Canadian cities, although the scan’s wording is partly obscured. The book’s own uncertainty matters: it supports the existence of organized settlement assistance, but does not permit a precise reconstruction of every location or the exact form of help.

The network’s reach was not limited to New York. The memorial book names landsleit groups in cities including Chicago, Philadelphia, Milwaukee, Los Angeles, Newark, Paterson and Detroit, as well as Montreal and Toronto. It also remembers the [Bialystoker Stimme](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_a2fb1c04bb2aa7c3caf15a73) as a publication that connected people across countries and carried news and memory between survivors and earlier émigrés. The book’s portrait is of a community held together not by a single organization alone, but by overlapping committees, local groups and shared communications.

A useful thread for further research is the committee’s early home at [246 East Broadway](research:What records survive of the Bialystoker Relief Committee at 246 East Broadway?). The memorial book identifies the address, but the material presented here does not establish how long the committee remained there or what records document its daily operations.

## The 1949 convention: gathering and rebuilding

The community’s most visible international gathering came on August 21–22, 1949, when, according to the memorial book, 277 delegates attended a New York convention called by the Bialystoker Center. The book presents the event both as a [Bialystok landsleit world convention](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_0368004827ff22e1bf591c6d) and as a [World Conference of Bialystok Jews in New York](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_3065e86de4c966a06a55657a). These descriptions refer to the same 1949 gathering, not separate conferences. The account says delegates represented organizations across the United States and Canada and from twelve other countries.

David Sohn was central to the convention as an organizer and speaker; the memorial book describes him as its leader and records his appeal at the closing. Zvi Klementinovski, an Israeli delegate and advocate for the project, argued for building a Bialystoker community in Israel. The book says the convention endorsed [Kiryat Bialystok](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_70966fe1a94b6c9cf895bd58), and that $100,000 was raised on the spot in cash and pledges. The gathering joined practical reconstruction to commemoration: a new settlement could provide homes for survivors while publicly carrying the name of a destroyed community.

The book also recalls the convention’s call for organizations from nearby towns to join the project and its greeting to Jews still living in Białystok. That detail complicates any simple account of a community that existed only abroad. The postwar network imagined kinship across borders: with survivors in Europe, with landsleit in North America and elsewhere, and with people building new lives in Israel.

## Different places, different forms of help

The Israeli organization described in the memorial book was established in 1946 to help newcomers find work and obtain financial assistance or loans. It later pursued the settlement project. In New York, the Center and Relief Committee supported survivors arriving in America and people elsewhere; in smaller American and Canadian cities, local landsleit groups maintained community ties. These were related efforts, but they were not interchangeable. A center in New York could coordinate funds and gatherings; a local association could offer companionship and help nearby; an Israeli organization could focus on settlement and livelihoods.

The book names people connected with these efforts, including David Sohn and Zvi Klementinovski. It also lists contributors and community figures such as Dr. Szymon Datner and Pejsach Bursztejn in connection with the Israel project. The records provided here do not supply enough evidence to reconstruct each person’s family, migration route or postwar fate, and those relationships should not be inferred from names alone.

The independent record offers a broader view of why such assistance mattered. The USHMM’s survivor history describes postwar Białystok as a place where survivors sought one another out, shared scarce necessities and re-formed bonds of friendship and mutual support. Its account is not testimony about the Bialystoker Center, but it illuminates the wider conditions in which landsleit networks operated. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/life-after-the-holocaust-aron-and-lisa-derman?utm_source=openai)) Yad Vashem’s encyclopedia entry on Białystok likewise provides the historical frame of a substantial prewar community destroyed under occupation; it does not independently verify the Center’s particular activities or the convention’s figures. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=130&utm_source=openai))

## Memory as a living connection

The memorial book looks beyond the immediate postwar years to a 1970 gathering of Białystok Jews in Israel. The [First World Gathering of Bialystok Jews](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_1d4f4187ac2a6c4b769b48a6) suggests that organized remembrance continued after the convention and the founding of Kiryat Bialystok. The book’s account is written from within the community, and its language of continuity expresses how survivors and landsleit understood their work: as care for one another and as a way to keep the destroyed hometown present.

That is the memorial book’s particular contribution. It records not only organizations and resolutions but a community’s own explanation of why they mattered. The wider sources establish the catastrophe and the difficult postwar landscape; the book shows how Białystokers tried to answer that rupture with relief, gathering, settlement and memory. Its narrative cannot represent every survivor or every relative scattered across the world. But it preserves the names, institutions and ambitions through which one dispersed community sought to remain a community.
